issues.legal_issue: A special family custom that modifies ordinary succession law must be proved by evidence confined to the custom pleaded and sufficient to establish that the custom was consistently followed and accepted as the governing rule.
material_facts: The claim to inherit depended on a special family custom because the claimants would not inherit under ordinary succession law.
The pleadings identified the custom as prevailing in a particular family, but evidence was offered about many other branches descended from a remote ancestor.
Only three of the claimed instances related to the family identified in the pleadings, and the Court found those instances unproved.
Documents and the claimants’ conduct in earlier proceedings were inconsistent with their awareness of, or reliance on, the alleged custom.
issues.conclusion: The alleged custom was not established, and the claimants were not entitled to succeed on its basis.
issues.legal_principle: The party asserting a special custom bears the initial burden of proving it. A custom modifying ordinary succession law must have been acted upon for such a period and with such invariability that it was accepted by common consent as the governing rule; the evidence must be clear and unambiguous. Family-custom evidence may include family members’ consensus, traditional beliefs, statements and conduct, and need not consist of numerous instances. Evidence cannot travel beyond the pleadings. The Court applied Ramalakshmi Ammal v. Sivanatha Perumal Sethuraya (14 M.I.A. 570, 585), followed Pushpavathi Vijayaram v. P. Visweswar (AIR 1964 SC 118), and referred to Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona (45 I.A. 10; AIR 1917 PC 181).

rule.if: family_custom_succession_claim and custom_confined_to_pleaded_family and only_three_relevant_instances and relevant_instances_unproved and conduct_inconsistent_with_custom

predicates.family_custom_succession_claim: The claimants sought succession on the basis of a special family custom rather than ordinary succession rules.
predicates.custom_confined_to_pleaded_family: The pleadings identified a particular family as the family in which the asserted custom prevailed.
predicates.only_three_relevant_instances: Only three of the instances offered to prove the custom concerned the family identified in the pleadings.
predicates.relevant_instances_unproved: The evidence did not establish the instances concerning the pleaded family.
predicates.conduct_inconsistent_with_custom: The claimants’ documents and conduct in earlier proceedings were inconsistent with their having relied on or recognized the asserted custom.

issues.definition: When a succession claim based on a family custom is confined by the pleadings to a particular family, only three relevant instances are offered and those instances are unproved, and the claimants’ conduct is inconsistent with the custom, the custom is not established.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate as to a deceased claimant’s estate merely because one of the estate’s legal representatives was not added, where another legal representative is already on record and there is no fraud or collusion affecting the omitted representative.
material_facts: A claimant died during the proceedings, and his widow and son were brought on record.
After the widow died, her son remained on record, but her daughter was not added as a legal representative.
The claimants held individual shares that could have been pursued separately.
There was no fraud or collusion between the parties on record to prejudice the omitted daughter.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the daughter did not cause the appeal to abate because the deceased widow’s estate was represented by her son already on record.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 22, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the governing principle is whether the deceased’s estate is represented, not whether every legal representative has been impleaded. In the absence of fraud or collusion, a legal representative on record may represent the estate, including the interests of omitted representatives. The Court relied on Daya Ram v. Shyam Sundari, Dolai Molliko v. K. C. Patnaik, Mahabir Prasad v. Jage Ram, and related decisions, and distinguished cases such as State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram and Rameshwar Prasad v. M/s. Shyam Beharilal Jagannath, which concerned materially different circumstances, including an estate with no representative on record or an indivisible decree.

rule.if: appeal_continued_after_claimant_death and deceased_claimant_had_individual_share and another_legal_representative_on_record and no_fraud_or_collusion_against_omitted_representative

predicates.appeal_continued_after_claimant_death: An appeal remained pending after a claimant died during the proceedings.
predicates.deceased_claimant_had_individual_share: The deceased claimant had a specific share that could have been pursued separately from the shares of the other claimants.
predicates.another_legal_representative_on_record: At least one legal representative of the deceased claimant or successor to the deceased representative’s interest was already a party to the proceedings.
predicates.no_fraud_or_collusion_against_omitted_re: The parties on record did not act fraudulently or in collusion to prejudice the legal representative who was not added.

issues.definition: When an appeal continues after the death of a claimant with an individual share, another legal representative is on record, and there is no fraud or collusion against an omitted representative, the appeal does not abate as to the estate.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may grant relief to appellants in related appeals despite the omission of a claimant as a respondent in some appeals when the claimant’s interest is separate, another appeal includes that claimant, and the omission resulted from oversight.
material_facts: A trial decree awarded separate shares to multiple claimants, each of whom could have sued for an individual share.
Three appeals were filed against the decree; one included the claimant who was omitted as a respondent in the other two.
The appellants in the appeals with the omission had filed appeals to establish their rights, and the omission occurred through oversight.
The separate interests meant that the decree could be varied as to some claimants without producing conflicting decrees.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could allow the appeal that included the omitted claimant and, under its appellate powers, grant relief to the appellants in the other appeals as well.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, rules 4 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit an appellate court, in appropriate circumstances, to grant relief to parties who have not appealed or whose appeal has a procedural defect. Their application depends on the nature of the decree and the parties’ interests. Where the decree is in substance a combination of separate decrees for individual shares, omission of one claimant as a respondent in some appeals does not prevent relief in an appeal in which that claimant is a party, and relief may be extended to appellants in the related appeals where the omission was an oversight. The Court relied on Ratan Lal v. Lal Man Das, Karam Singh Sobti v. Shri Pratap Chand, and the discussion in Krishna Reddy v. Ramireddi, and distinguished cases involving common and indivisible interests.

rule.if: appeal_against_multi_claimant_decree and claimants_have_separate_interests and related_appeal_includes_omitted_claimant and appellants_filed_related_appeals and omission_was_oversight

predicates.appeal_against_multi_claimant_decree: An appeal challenged a decree made in a proceeding involving multiple claimants.
predicates.claimants_have_separate_interests: Each claimant had a distinct share that could have been pursued separately, and relief concerning one share would not necessarily affect the others.
predicates.related_appeal_includes_omitted_claimant: At least one related appeal included as a party the claimant omitted from another appeal.
predicates.appellants_filed_related_appeals: The parties seeking relief had filed appeals to challenge the decree.
predicates.omission_was_oversight: The failure to include the claimant as a respondent in some appeals occurred through oversight rather than because the appellants chose not to appeal.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a decree involving claimants with separate interests, a related appeal includes the claimant omitted from another appeal, the affected appellants filed related appeals, and the omission was an oversight, appellate relief may extend to those appellants.
